summary: Defines the SRv6 network programming framework, where an operator or application encodes a sequence of instructions in the IPv6 packet header. Each instruction is identified by a Segment Identifier in the packet and carried out by one or more network nodes, and the document defines a set of basic instructions.

plainLanguage.summary: Packets carry a to-do list in their header, and routers along the way each do their step, so the sender controls the journey.

questions: what does the end behavior do in srv6
subtitle: Turning IPv6 addresses into instructions: a catalogue of behaviors that routers run when a packet names them.

tldr.problem: Operators and applications want to steer packets through a chosen path and have the network perform services such as VPN delivery along the way, not just forward by destination.
tldr.mechanism: An SRv6 Segment Identifier (SID) is an IPv6 address split into locator, function and argument. The function is bound to a behavior such as End, End.X or End.DT4, and the packet's header lists the SIDs to visit in order.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the base set of endpoint and headend behaviors, their pseudocode, a flavor mechanism and an IANA registry of 16-bit behavior codepoints so overlays can interoperate.

today: RFC 8986 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of these SRv6 behaviors.

sections.title: SRv6 Network Programming
sections.content:
Segment Routing (RFC 8402) is a source-routing approach: an ingress node steers a packet through an ordered list of instructions called segments. Each segment stands for a function to be called at a specific place in the network, and a function is defined locally on the node that runs it. It can be as simple as moving to the next segment or as complex as a user-defined behavior.

Network Programming combines such functions to reach goals beyond plain routing. RFC 8986 defines the concept for IPv6 and specifies the main behaviors that allow interoperable overlays with underlay optimization. Familiarity with the Segment Routing Header (RFC 8754) is expected.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a letter is just delivered to an address. Here the letter also carries a list of errands, and each post office on the way does one errand.

sections.title: The SRv6 SID
sections.content:
An SRv6 SID is an IPv6 address. When it sits in the destination address of a packet, transit nodes route it like any IPv6 address. The RFC structures it as LOC:FUNCT:ARG: a locator in the L most significant bits, then F bits of function and A bits of argument. The lengths are flexible as long as L+F+A is at most 128, and any remaining bits MUST be zero.

The locator can be written B:N, where B is the operator's SID block and N identifies the node that instantiates the SID. The function is an opaque identifier of a local behavior. The argument can carry extra information such as flow or service data; its format is defined by the behavior. The ARG value of a routed SID SHOULD stay constant within a flow, since varying it may change ECMP hashing and cause reordering.

A source node cannot work out the behavior from the function bits. The node therefore advertises each SID in the control plane together with an SRv6 Endpoint Behavior codepoint. A SID is routed if it falls within an IPv6 prefix advertised by a routing protocol, and non-routed otherwise. A non-routed SID can be reached by preceding it in the SID list with a routed SID of the same node or with an Adj-SID.

The RFC gives a worked example: block 2001:db8:bbbb::/48, Router 3 with locator 2001:db8:bbbb:3::/64, and function 0x0100 bound to End.X, advertised as 2001:db8:bbbb:3:100:: with behavior codepoint 5.
sections.plainLanguage: The address is like a street, a house number and a note: the street finds the right building, the house number picks what the building should do, and the note gives extra details.

sections.title: Endpoint Behaviors
sections.content:
When a node receives a packet whose destination address matches a locally instantiated SID, it runs the behavior bound to that SID. The base behavior is End, the SRv6 form of a Prefix-SID. In the RFC's pseudocode, if Segments Left is 0 it stops processing the SRH; if the Hop Limit is 1 or less it sends an ICMP Time Exceeded message and discards the packet; otherwise it decrements the Hop Limit and Segments Left, copies the next SID from the segment list into the destination address and looks the packet up for forwarding.

End.X sends the packet to one of a set of Layer 3 adjacencies and is the SRv6 form of an Adj-SID. End.T does the lookup in a specific IPv6 table. The decapsulating family is used at the last segment of a policy, and each such SID MUST be the last segment. End.DX6 and End.DX4 remove the outer IPv6 header and forward to a Layer 3 adjacency, equivalent to a per-CE VPN label. End.DT6, End.DT4 and End.DT46 remove it and look up a specific table, equivalent to a per-VRF VPN label.

For Layer 2, End.DX2 forwards the exposed Ethernet frame to an outgoing interface, End.DX2V looks up VLANs in an L2 table, End.DT2U learns and looks up MAC addresses, and End.DT2M floods within an L2 table using an argument that excludes certain interfaces. Binding behaviors let a SID stand for a whole policy: End.B6.Encaps pushes a new IPv6 header with its own SRH, End.B6.Encaps.Red leaves the first SID out of the SRH, and End.BM binds to an SR-MPLS policy. Upper-layer headers at an End SID are only processed if local configuration allows, and the RFC recommends allowing only types that are not forwarded, such as ICMPv6 (type 58).
sections.plainLanguage: Each router has a menu of jobs: pass it along, hand it to a specific neighbor, open the envelope and deliver what is inside, or swap in a whole new list of errands.

sections.title: Flavors: PSP, USP and USD
sections.content:
Three flavors modify the End, End.X and End.T behaviors, individually or combined. A node that offers a flavored and an unflavored version advertises them as different SIDs with different behavior codepoints, and advertises PSP only if the operator enables it.

PSP (Penultimate Segment Pop) removes the SRH at the penultimate segment endpoint, the node that copies the last SID into the destination address and takes Segments Left from one to zero. This lets the egress node parse and remove fewer bytes. PSP does not increase the packet's MTU, so it has no impact on Path MTU discovery.

USP (Ultimate Segment Pop) removes the SRH when Segments Left is already 0, before handing the packet on; the RFC cites packets destined to hosts with smartNICs. USD (Ultimate Segment Decapsulation) lets End, End.X or End.T decapsulate an inner IPv4 or IPv6 packet; the RFC cites Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate (TI-LFA) repair paths as an application.
sections.plainLanguage: PSP means the second-to-last stop throws away the used errand list so the last stop has less to read. USD means the last stop opens the outer envelope and delivers the inner one.

sections.title: Headend Behaviors
sections.content:
Headend behaviors run at the node that steers packets into an SR Policy. H.Encaps pushes an outer IPv6 header with its own SRH, sets the outer source address to the node's own address T and the outer destination to the first SID, copies or computes the outer header fields as in RFC 2473 and RFC 6437, decrements the inner Hop Limit or TTL, and forwards. The received packet is otherwise encapsulated unmodified. It works for any L3 traffic and is commonly used for L3VPN.

H.Encaps.Red shortens the SRH by leaving the first SID only in the destination address. H.Encaps.L2 encapsulates a received Ethernet frame, with its Next Header set to 143, and removes the preamble and frame check sequence on the way in. The decapsulating node MUST regenerate them. H.Encaps.L2.Red is the reduced variant. For each, the SRH MAY be omitted when the policy has only one segment and needs no flag, tag or TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: The first router puts the whole packet into a new envelope and writes the list of stops on the outside, so the packet travels exactly the route it was given.

sections.title: Control Plane, Counters and Hashing
sections.content:
A node supporting the RFC SHOULD keep a pair of counters (packets and bytes) per local SID for traffic processed successfully. Packets that generate ICMP errors or are dropped are not counted.

When a flow-based choice among several paths is needed, the outer IPv6 source address, destination address and flow label MUST be part of the hash. This applies to ECMP lookups, End.X, End.DX4 or End.DX6 bound to several adjacencies, and SR Policy paths with multiple SID lists.

The RFC also gives an illustrative overview of the control plane. End, End.T and End.X SIDs, with their flavors, are expected in the IGP, which should also advertise each node's Maximum SID Depth. BGP-LS advertises the SRv6 capabilities, locators and SIDs of nodes to controllers. The decapsulating VPN behaviors End.DX4, End.DX6, End.DT4, End.DT6, End.DT46, End.DX2, End.DX2V, End.DT2U and End.DT2M can be signaled in BGP. An egress PE that wants to hide the behavior can use the Opaque codepoint. A SID in the IGP does not change routing reachability, which is governed by locator prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers count how many packets each errand handled, and they tell the rest of the network which errands they can do.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 8986 introduces no new security considerations beyond those of Segment Routing (RFC 8402) and the SRH (RFC 8754). It relies on a well-defined trust boundary around the SR domain, so that SRv6 services serve internal traffic while external traffic cannot access or exploit them. The RFC asks for care in allocating SID addresses separately from end-user addresses.

RFC 8754 defines an HMAC TLV so that nodes can verify that the SRH was selected by an authorized party and not modified. The behaviors here have the same HMAC TLV handling and mutability properties for the Flags, Tag and Segment List fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The errand list should only be trusted inside your own neighborhood, and you can add a seal so nobody changes the list on the way.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA allocated the value 143 for Ethernet in the Assigned Internet Protocol Numbers registry. In the Next Header field it means the payload is an Ethernet frame.

IANA also created a top-level Segment Routing registry and an "SRv6 Endpoint Behaviors" subregistry of 16-bit identifiers. These identifiers are not encoded in the function bits of a SID. Values 1 to 32767 are First Come First Served, 32768 to 34815 are Private Use, and 0, 34816 to 65534 are reserved, with 65535 reserved as Opaque. Initial entries include End (1), End.X (5), End.T (9), End.B6.Encaps (14), End.BM (15), End.DX6 (16), End.DX4 (17), End.DT6 (18), End.DT4 (19), End.DT46 (20) and End.DX2 (21), with flavored variants of End, End.X and End.T in between.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list that gives each errand a number, so every router and controller means the same thing by it.

viz.caption: THE THREE PARTS OF AN SRV6 SID

items.title: LOC (L bits)
items.text: Locator: routable prefix leading to the node that instantiates the SID.

items.title: FUNCT (F bits)
items.text: Opaque identifier of a local behavior bound to the SID.

items.title: ARG (A bits)
items.text: Optional arguments for the behavior. L+F+A is at most 128; leftover bits are zero.

items.label: End
items.desc: Endpoint; SRv6 form of a Prefix-SID.

items.label: End.T
items.desc: Endpoint with specific IPv6 table lookup.

items.label: End.B6.Encaps
items.desc: Bound to an SRv6 Policy with encapsulation.

items.label: Opaque
items.desc: Hides the specific behavior from other routers.

viz.caption: PACKET P1 AFTER H.ENCAPS AND H.ENCAPS.RED (RFC 8986, SECTIONS 5.1-5.2)

data.title: Notation (SA,DA) (SID list; SL) (inner packet)
data.code:
H.Encaps:      (T, S1) (S3, S2, S1; SL=2) (A, B2)
H.Encaps.Red:  (T, S1) (S3, S2; SL=2) (A, B2)
